820.title: Joel: old men shall dream (Joel 3:1)
820.hook: the spirit poured on all: "your old men shall dream dreams"
820.howItsDone: Joel is one of the Twelve in the Hebrew Bible; Jews read Joel 2 as part of the haftarah on Shabbat Shuvah in some communities, alongside Hosea 14.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea's last chapter: return, and bring words with you. Your line was take with you words. Today, the second voice on the scroll of the Twelve.

Who gets to dream? The book of Joel opens with a disaster. Locusts, wave after wave, stripping the vines and the fig trees bare, until the fields mourn and the offerings stop. Joel calls for fasting, for gathering, for turning back. Rend your heart, he says, and not your garments. And then, after the ruin and the return, a promise comes that has nothing to do with crops. It's about who gets to see the future.
screen: `WHO GETS TO DREAM?` → `LOCUSTS STRIP THE LAND.` → `THEN A PROMISE ABOUT SEEING.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions." All flesh, and then the text names who that includes. Sons and daughters. The old and the young. And in the next verse, the servants and the handmaids, the people at the bottom of the household. In Jewish Bibles this opens chapter three; in the King James it ends chapter two. Same words. Now notice the old men. They aren't told to remember, or to advise, or to step aside for the young. They dream. Here, dreaming isn't the property of the young with their whole lives ahead. The spirit comes to the old, and gives them something new to see. In the Torah, Moses hears that two men are prophesying in the camp, away from the tent where the elders gathered, and Joshua asks him to stop them. His answer, in the King James words: "would God that all the LORD's people were prophets." Joel's promise reads like that wish coming true. Not one prophet on a mountain, but a whole people, any age, any rank, the spirit poured out like rain on a field the locusts left bare. Joel doesn't say what the old men will dream. Only that they will.
screen: `UPON ALL FLESH.` · `SONS, DAUGHTERS, SERVANTS, HANDMAIDS.` · then, large: `YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM DREAMS.` · then: `WOULD GOD THAT ALL WERE PROPHETS.`

segments.voice: Whatever your age, there may be a voice somewhere that says it's too late, or too early, or not for someone like you; set it down for a while and let one dream come, a skill, a trip, a kindness, a thing you'd like to build or mend. Don't plan it, just let yourself see it, the way Joel promises the old will dream. If you pray, you can hold it before God.

Your line: old men dream dreams. Any age, any rank. Day eight hundred twenty, done.

821.title: Amos: justice as waters (Amos 5:24)
821.hook: "let justice well up as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream"
821.howItsDone: Amos is one of the Twelve; his call for justice is quoted in Jewish teaching on tzedakah and social justice, and Jews give tzedakah as a regular practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joel's promise of a spirit poured out on all flesh, young and old. Your line was old men dream dreams. Today, a voice from the same scroll with no patience for pretty music.

The festival is in full swing. Crowds at the sanctuary, offerings on the altar, the sound of harps and singing. Everything looks devout. And into the middle of it walks Amos, with a message that stops the music. In the King James words, God says: "I hate, I despise your feast days." And then: "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs." Noise. The holy songs, called noise. What could make worship sound like that?
screen: `THE FESTIVAL IN FULL SWING.` → `I HATE, I DESPISE YOUR FEAST DAYS.` → `THE SONGS CALLED NOISE.`

segments.voice: Amos has already told them. The same people singing at the altar are selling the needy for a pair of shoes, turning justice into wormwood, pushing the poor aside in the gate, where the courts sat. The feast and the cheating can't live in the same house. Then comes the line Amos is remembered for, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "But let justice well up as waters, And righteousness as a mighty stream." Two Hebrew words carry it. Mishpat, justice: a fair ruling, the poor person's case heard. And tzedakah, righteousness, the word Jews also use for giving to those in need. And the picture is water: not a trickle, a mighty stream. The Hebrew for that stream is nachal eitan, and some readers hear in eitan a stream that never runs dry, unlike streambeds that run only after rain and then go to dust. Read that way, Amos asks for the other kind: justice that doesn't show up once a year at a festival and dry out, but runs in every season, through the market, the courts and the ordinary day. It would be easy to hear this as a rejection of prayer and festivals. Jews kept praying, kept the festivals, and kept reading Amos. One way to hear the prophet: worship without justice is noise, and justice makes the song worth hearing.
screen: `SELLING THE NEEDY FOR A PAIR OF SHOES.` · `MISHPAT AND TZEDAKAH.` · then, large: `LET JUSTICE WELL UP AS WATERS.` · then: `A STREAM THAT KEEPS ON FLOWING.`

segments.voice: Let your mind walk through the places your day touches, the store, the job, the group chat, the street outside, and look for someone who's been pushed aside: an unpaid bill you owe, a coworker who never gets credit, a neighbor nobody checks on, a cause you've meant to give to. Let one come clearly, and choose one just act, small enough for today. If you pray, you can ask for justice to flow through your hands.

822.title: Amos: just a herdsman (Amos 7:14–15)
822.hook: "I was no prophet... but I was a herdman", and was sent anyway
822.howItsDone: Amos is read as one of the Twelve, and passages from his book are read as haftarot in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amos called the festival songs noise and asked for justice to well up like waters. Your line was justice like waters. Today, someone in charge tells Amos to go home.

Bethel, the royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom. Amos has been speaking hard words there about the king and the land, and the priest in charge, Amaziah, has had enough. He sends word to the king that Amos is conspiring. Then he turns to Amos himself: go, flee back to Judah, earn your bread there, prophesy there. In the King James words: "prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel." Who do you think you are?
screen: `BETHEL, THE KING'S SANCTUARY.` → `GO HOME TO JUDAH.` → `WHO DO YOU THINK YOU ARE?`

segments.voice: Amos answers honestly. In the King James words: "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit." No credentials. No school. No family trade. Some readers take a prophet's son to mean a member of a prophetic circle, a trained disciple; either way, Amos says he was not one. He kept animals and tended sycamore figs, the plain fruit of a working countryside. Then the turn: "And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel." Not from a temple, not from a palace. From behind the animals, in the middle of an ordinary workday. He doesn't argue his qualifications or claim to be more than he is. He says, in effect: I'm not a professional, and I didn't choose this. I was sent. The authority isn't in his résumé. It's in the sending. And there's something quietly bold in it. Amaziah stands for the official sanctuary, the king's chapel. Amos stands for nothing but the message. His book opens the same way, naming him among the herdmen of Tekoa. The plain origin isn't hidden; it's the first thing we learn. Whoever kept these words chose to start with the herdsman.

segments.voice: Think of a place where you've stayed quiet because you weren't the expert, a meeting where something seemed wrong, a family decision, a friend who needed someone to say a hard thing, and let the old reasons rise: I'm not qualified, it's not my place, someone else will. Hold them, set them down gently, and picture yourself speaking anyway, in your own ordinary words, the way a herdsman would. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to say it.

823.title: Obadiah: don't gloat (Obadiah 1:12)
823.hook: do not look on your brother's disaster with pleasure
823.howItsDone: In some communities, Obadiah is read in synagogue as the haftarah with the Torah portion of Jacob and Esau, and at the Passover seder it is customary to spill drops of wine as the plagues are named.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amos: no prophet and no prophet's son, taken from behind the flock and sent. Your line was just a herdsman. Today, a prophet with one message for one neighbor, and a hard word about watching.

Jerusalem is under attack. Strangers are at the gates, carrying off what they can. And on the hills nearby, the neighbors are watching. Not helping. Watching. Some of them are pleased. A few come down to pick through the wreckage, and some stand at the crossroads to catch those trying to escape. The neighbors are Edom, and the book of Obadiah is written to them. In the story of Genesis, Edom comes from Esau. Which makes them family: Jacob's brother.
screen: `THE CITY UNDER ATTACK.` → `THE NEIGHBORS WATCHING.` → `EDOM, THE BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Obadiah's word to Edom is a list of what they shouldn't have done, and it moves step by step, like a slow camera. In the King James words: "thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress." Looking. Then rejoicing. Then speaking proudly. The next verses go further: entering the gate, laying hands on the goods, standing at the crossroads. Gloating isn't the last step. It's one of the first. It starts with the eyes and the heart, long before the hands. And the reason the text gives is family: "For thy violence against thy brother Jacob," the book says, shame shall cover thee. Jewish teaching carries the same thread elsewhere. Proverbs says, in the King James words: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." Not even an enemy. And the Talmud tells a story about the sea closing over the Egyptians: the angels want to sing, and God stops them. The works of my hands are drowning, God says, and you want to sing? Some families remember this at the Passover table, spilling drops of wine as the plagues are named. A people rescued, and still not gloating.

segments.voice: Let your mind be honest for a moment: is there someone whose trouble would be a little satisfying to hear about, a rival, an ex, a public figure, a coworker who wronged you? Without judging yourself, notice that first small pleasure, the looking at the top of Obadiah's list, and hold that person as someone's family, someone's brother or sister; you don't have to like them, just put the gloating down. If you pray, you can pray for them.

824.title: Jonah runs (Jonah 1)
824.hook: the prophet flees to Tarshish and ends up in the sea
824.howItsDone: Jews read the whole book of Jonah as the haftarah at the afternoon service of Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Obadiah told Edom it should never have watched its brother's disaster with pleasure. Your line was don't gloat. Today, a prophet who is told to go, and goes the other way.

The word of the LORD comes to Jonah, son of Amittai, and it's clear. In the King James words: "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it." Jonah arises. That part he does. Then the very next verse: "But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD." Nineveh is one direction. Tarshish is across the sea, the other way. He walks down to the port of Joppa, finds a ship, pays the fare, and climbs aboard.
screen: `ARISE, GO TO NINEVEH.` → `HE RISES TO FLEE.` → `A SHIP TO TARSHISH.`

segments.voice: Follow Jonah's feet, and the chapter keeps taking him down. Down to Joppa. Down into the ship. And when the storm hits, he has already gone down into the sides of the ship, the lowest part, and the King James says "he lay, and was fast asleep." Some readers hear running away as a kind of sinking. Up on deck, everyone else is awake and terrified. Each sailor cries to his own god. They throw the cargo overboard. The captain finds Jonah asleep below and shakes him: get up, call on your God. The sailors cast lots, and the lot falls on Jonah. Who are you, they ask, where are you from? His answer lands with a sharp irony: "I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land." The God he's running from made the very water under the ship. You can't outrun someone who made the road. Then the sailors, who don't share his faith, are the ones who fight to save him. Jonah tells them to throw him into the sea. They don't. They row hard for land, and can't make it. Only then, praying not to be held guilty, do they cast him in. The sea goes still. And Jonah, who kept going down, is as far down as a man can go, with the chapter not yet done with him.
screen: `DOWN TO JOPPA, DOWN INTO THE SHIP.` · `ASLEEP IN THE STORM.` · then, large: `THE GOD WHICH HATH MADE THE SEA.` · then: `THE SAILORS TRY TO SAVE HIM.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, without blame, what you've been sailing away from: an email you haven't opened, a conversation you keep postponing, a doctor's appointment, a call you know you need to make. Let one come up from the bottom of the ship, and don't solve it; just stop moving away from it for a while, and turn to face it the way you'd face the shore. If you pray, you can bring it before God.

825.title: Out of the belly (Jonah 2)
825.hook: from inside the fish, Jonah prays
825.howItsDone: Jonah's prayer is read in synagogue as part of the book of Jonah on Yom Kippur afternoon, and its lines echo the language of the Psalms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah ran for Tarshish, slept through the storm, and went over the side. Your line was you can't outrun it. Today, Jonah is somewhere he can't run from at all.

Inside the fish there is no sky, no shore, no way to tell the hour. The text gives the whole thing in one plain sentence. In the King James words: "Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights." A prophet who ran as far as he could has run out of places to go. And there, of all places, Jonah prays.
screen: `NO SKY, NO SHORE.` → `A GREAT FISH, PREPARED.` → `THERE, JONAH PRAYS.`

segments.voice: "Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly." And what he says is surprising. It isn't mainly a plea to get out. It sounds more like a psalm of thanks. "I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice." Belly of hell, in the King James. The Hebrew word is Sheol, which the 1917 Jewish translation renders the nether-world. Jonah is inside a fish, and he describes it as the bottom of the world. All thy billows and thy waves passed over me. The weeds were wrapped about my head. I went down to the bottoms of the mountains. Down again, the direction he's gone since Joppa. Then the prayer turns: "When my soul fainted within me I remembered the LORD." Notice the tense. He speaks of being heard while still inside. Some readers find a strange hope in that: thanks before the rescue, from the low place itself. It ends on a short line, "Salvation is of the LORD." Then, the text says plainly, the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land. No ceremony. Just dry ground under his feet. The man who kept going down finally calls up, and he does it without waiting to climb out first.
screen: `A PRAYER FROM INSIDE THE FISH.` · `THE BELLY OF SHEOL, THE BOTTOM OF THE WORLD.` · then, large: `WHEN MY SOUL FAINTED, I REMEMBERED.` · then: `UP ON THE DRY LAND.`

segments.voice: Name, quietly, where you are right now, not where you hope to be: tired, stuck, worried, grieving, or simply fine, and don't wait to feel better before you speak; Jonah didn't. If you pray, you can use his own words: I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me. If you don't, just say plainly, to yourself, what the low place is like.
Sheol. Hebrew for the nether-world: Jonah's prayer from inside the fish, from the low place, before he's out. Today's word.
Your line: heard before he was out. Thanks, from the low place itself. Day eight hundred twenty-five, done.

826.title: Should I not have pity? (Jonah 4)
826.hook: God asks Jonah: should I not pity Nineveh, and much cattle too?
826.carry: doest thou well to be angry
826.howItsDone: Jews read the whole book of Jonah at the afternoon service of Yom Kippur, ending with God's question about pity for Nineveh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah prayed from inside the fish. Your line was heard before he was out. Today, his story ends, and it ends on a question.

Jonah finally goes to Nineveh and cries out that the great city will be overthrown. And it works. The people believe. They fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The king comes down from his throne and sits in ashes. God sees them turn from their evil way, and doesn't bring the disaster. A whole city spared. A prophet might be expected to rejoice. In the King James words: "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry."
screen: `JONAH GOES TO NINEVEH.` → `THE CITY TURNS.` → `AND JONAH IS VERY ANGRY.`

segments.voice: Now we learn why he ran. Jonah tells God, in the King James words: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil." He quotes God's mercy back at God, as a complaint: he knew the city would be forgiven, and didn't want it. God answers with a question: doest thou well to be angry? Jonah doesn't answer. He goes out east of the city, builds a little shelter, and sits to watch. God makes a plant grow over him for shade, a kikayon, a gourd in the King James, and Jonah is exceedingly glad of it. Next dawn, a worm attacks it and it withers. A hot east wind blows, the sun beats on his head, and Jonah says he'd rather die. Then God speaks the book's last words: "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night:" And: "And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?" The 1917 Jewish translation has: should not I have pity. And the book stops. We never hear Jonah's answer; the question is left for whoever reads it next. Even the animals are in it: God's pity reaches the cattle of a foreign city. On Yom Kippur afternoon, Jews read this whole book, and it ends right here.
screen: `GRACIOUS, MERCIFUL, SLOW TO ANGER.` · `A GOURD THAT GREW AND WITHERED.` · then, large: `SHOULD NOT I HAVE PITY ON NINEVEH?` · then: `THE BOOK ENDS ON A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Let your circle of good wishes go one step out, toward someone from a place or group you'd rather not see spared, a city in the news, a rival team, the far side of an argument, though not someone who wronged you. You don't have to agree with them; just let God's question to Jonah be asked about them: should there be no pity here? If you pray, you can pray for their good.
